case_name: CASE OF MLADINA D.D. LJUBLJANA v. SLOVENIA (No. 2)

assessment.1. Existence of an interference: There was clearly an interference with the applicant company’s freedom of expression. The magazine published a satirical article and two side-by-side family photographs in its “Mladinamit” section (see paragraphs 8-9). Following civil proceedings brought by B.G., the domestic courts ordered the applicant company to publish a judgment and an apology (see paragraph 17) and later to pay damages, ultimately reduced to EUR 3,000 plus interest (see paragraphs 25, 28 and 30). Such civil sanctions are restrictions on press freedom within the meaning of Article 10. The fact that the impugned expression was political and satirical reinforces that Article 10 is engaged, as in political-speech cases concerning criticism of politicians (see no. 20981/10).

assessment.2. Lawfulness of the interference: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law. The domestic courts relied on constitutional protections of dignity, privacy and personality rights, alongside freedom of expression (see paragraph 32), and on Articles 178 and 179 of the Code of Obligations, which expressly allow publication of a judgment, retraction-type remedies and compensation for non-pecuniary damage where personality rights are infringed (see paragraph 33). The applicant company was able to contest the claim before three judicial levels, including the Constitutional Court (see paragraphs 15-24). On the facts provided, the legal basis was accessible and foreseeable enough for a publisher to understand that publication of a highly offensive comparison involving a politician’s family and minor children could trigger civil liability.

assessment.3. Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued legitimate aims recognised by Article 10 § 2, above all the protection of the reputation or rights of others. B.G.’s claim was framed as one concerning honour, good name, dignity and the negative impact of the comparison on him and his family (see paragraph 13). The domestic courts ultimately accepted that, even if the textual criticism of B.G. as a politician was protected, the visual comparison of his family with Joseph Goebbels’s family encroached on his personal sphere as a father and implicated the interests of his family, including young children (see paragraphs 18, 20, 23-24). That falls within the protection of the reputation and rights of others, in line with the Court’s approach in balancing press freedom against personal rights in cases concerning photographs and public figures (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08 and 60641/08; see also no. 40454/07).

assessment.4. Necessary in a democratic society: The decisive issue is proportionality. On one side, the publication contributed to an ongoing public debate about the political methods of B.G. and his party and the appropriateness of comparing him to Goebbels (see paragraphs 6-8, 15 and 23). B.G. was a prominent opposition politician and therefore had to tolerate particularly robust criticism (see paragraphs 5 and 15), and satire enjoys broad protection, a factor expressly acknowledged by the Supreme Court and the Constitutional Court (see paragraphs 20 and 24; see also no. 20981/10). On the other side, the domestic courts gave specific and relevant reasons for distinguishing the visual element from the textual political criticism. They found that the side-by-side images, identical in size and similar in composition, shifted the message from political methods to a comparison between two families (see paragraphs 18, 20, 23-24). That conclusion was strengthened by the captioning, the separate satirical section, and the risk that the average reader would not connect the photographs with the longer editorial explanation elsewhere in the magazine (see paragraphs 8-9 and 24). The involvement of minor children was central: even though the photograph had been taken at a public religious event and B.G. had previously exposed his family to media attention (see paragraphs 10, 12 and 15), the courts reasonably held that this did not amount to consent to reuse in any context, especially one invoking the symbolism of Joseph Goebbels and his family (see paragraph 24). Applying the criteria developed in the Court’s photograph cases—public interest, notoriety, prior conduct, content/form/consequences, and severity of sanction (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08 and 40454/07)—the national courts’ balancing appears careful and convincing. They did not condemn the political line of the publication as such; they limited liability to the family-photo comparison, and they moderated the sanction with explicit regard to chilling effects, reducing damages to EUR 3,000 (see paragraphs 27 and 30). In these circumstances, the interference was supported by relevant and sufficient reasons and was proportionate. I therefore predict that it would be regarded as necessary in a democratic society.
